name: Leg press
equipment: 45° plate-loaded leg press with adjustable bottom stops
plates (loaded by staff; from Good arm OK your uninjured hand loads plates of 10 kg or less)
why: Your main leg muscle-builder while the arm heals. The machine supports your back and needs no balance or hands, so you can train your biggest muscles hard and safely: that's where most of the muscle you regain first will come from, and strong quads and glutes carry you up (and, more importantly, down) long hills.
setup: Once, before your first session: ask staff to set the bottom safety stops at your bottom position (knees bent about 90°, lower back still flat on the pad) and to leave the top catches released. Note the hole number in your session notes.
Staff load the plates evenly. From Good arm OK, your uninjured hand may load and unload plates of 10 kg or less, one at a time, close to your body; staff do anything heavier.
Sit right back into the seat while the sled rests on the stops. Feet hip-width in the middle of the platform, toes turned out slightly.
Injured arm across your stomach, never on your thighs, a handle or a catch. Your uninjured hand takes the side handle only when you stand up.
Ramp-up: 10 easy box squats, so the plates don't change (from Phase 2a, lighter ramp-up sets on the press instead).
Log the plates you added (both sides together), the same way every time; note the sled's own weight once if it's posted.
cues: Press from the stops through your whole foot; heels stay down
Knees track over your second and third toes
Lower for 3 s until the sled just touches the stops, pause 1 s without relaxing
Breathe out as you push; no breath-holding
Stop just short of locking your knees
mistakes: Stops set so deep that your hips curl up and your lower back peels off the pad: raise them one hole.
Dropping the sled onto the stops and resting there between reps: touch lightly and keep the tension.
Knees caving inwards: slow down, push the knees out over the toes and take a little weight off.
Snapping the knees straight at the top: keep a soft knee so the muscles stay working.
arm_safety: On a 45° plate-loaded sled you use a dead start and never touch the catches: the sled rests on the bottom stops, which staff set once at your bottom position, and every set starts and finishes on them. Staff load and unload the plates until Good arm OK is set; after that your uninjured hand may load plates of 10 kg or less, one at a time, and staff do anything heavier. Getting in: sit down using your legs only, then slide back into the seat. Getting out: set the sled on the stops, put your feet down one at a time and stand up with your uninjured hand on the side handle. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed: never hands on your thighs, and never the injured hand on a handle. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you catch yourself bracing with it.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3 (1–2 from Phase 1 week 4), 3-s lowering; start around a load you could do for 15

name: Single-leg leg press
equipment: 45° plate-loaded leg press with adjustable bottom stops
plates (loaded by staff; from Good arm OK your uninjured hand loads plates of 10 kg or less)
why: Hiking is thousands of single-leg efforts in a row. This trains each leg on its own with no balance demand, so you can find and fix a weaker side and build single-leg strength safely before harder free-standing single-leg work.
setup: Same stops as the two-leg press: the sled rests on them between sets.
Load about 40–50% of your two-leg working weight: staff, or (from Good arm OK) your uninjured hand for plates of 10 kg or less.
Place one foot in the middle of the platform, in line with your hip. Rest the other foot on the frame or footrest, not dangling and not on the platform.
Injured arm across your stomach, never hands on your thighs; uninjured hand on the side handle when you stand up.
cues: Hips square, both sides of your bottom on the seat
Knee tracks over the middle toes
Lower under control until the sled just touches the stops
Breathe out as you push
Start with your weaker leg and match the reps on the other
mistakes: Pelvis twisting or one hip lifting: reduce the range and the load.
Too heavy, so the knee caves in: drop the weight until the knee stays in line with the toes.
Rushing the second leg: rest 30–60 s between sides so both get quality work.
arm_safety: Exactly as for the leg press: a dead start from the bottom stops, no catches, legs-only entry, and your uninjured hand on the side handle to stand up. The stops matter even more here, because one leg can fail suddenly, so use a load you could clearly do 2–3 more reps with. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you catch yourself bracing with it.
dose: 3 × 10–15 per leg, RIR 2–3, about 30 s between legs

name: Calf raise on the leg press
why: Your calves push you up every step of every hill and absorb the load on the way down, and this loads them heavily with no balance demand. On a plate-loaded 45° sled it needs the catches, so your plan uses single-leg calf raises instead; it becomes an option after grip clearance.
setup: After grip clearance only, on a 45° sled: sit back with your legs almost straight and a soft, unlocked knee.
Put the balls of your feet on the bottom edge of the platform, heels hanging off, feet hip-width.
Keep the safety catches engaged if the machine allows calf work with them on; start light and ask staff to show you.
cues: Lower until you feel a deep calf stretch and pause 1–2 s
Press up through the big toe to full tiptoe and squeeze 1 s
Knees stay soft and still; only the ankles move
Steady breathing, no bouncing
mistakes: Bouncing half reps: slow down and use the full range with a pause at the bottom.
Bending and straightening the knees to help: keep the knee angle fixed and use less weight.
Feet creeping down the platform so they slide: keep the balls of the feet firmly on the edge and recheck between sets.
arm_safety: Locked until grip clearance and not in your plan. Calf raises need your legs almost straight, so the dead-start stops can't catch the sled; you'd be relying on the catches, and those take both hands. After grip clearance, with both hands on the catch handles: catches engaged if the machine allows calf work with them on, grippy shoes, start light, and stop the set the moment your feet start to slide. Never grab at the platform.
dose: 3 × 12–15, 1–2 s pause in the stretch, RIR 2 (after grip clearance)

name: Leg extension
why: Long descents hammer the front of the knee, and strong quads are your knee armour. The leg extension isolates the quads with your back supported and no balance demand, and it adds muscle to the biggest part of your thigh.
setup: Adjust the backrest so your knee joint lines up with the machine's pivot (usually marked with a dot).
Set the shin pad on the front of your lower shin, just above the ankles.
Set the start angle so your knees bend to about 90°, deeper only if it's comfortable.
Sit tall with your uninjured hand lightly on the side handle and your injured arm resting on your thigh or across your stomach.
cues: Straighten the knees smoothly; no kicking
Squeeze your thighs hard for 1 s at the top
Lower for 3 s
Breathe out as you lift
Keep your bottom on the seat
mistakes: Swinging the weight up: reduce the load and pause at the top.
Knee not lined up with the pivot, so the pad slides up the shin: adjust the backrest before the first set.
Hips lifting off the seat: lower the load and sit back into the pad.
arm_safety: Getting in: sit on the seat first, then swing your legs under the shin pad one at a time. Adjust the backrest, the shin pad and the weight pin with your uninjured hand (ask staff if a pin is stiff). Getting out: lift your legs out from under the pad one at a time and stand up using your legs. Arm: on your thigh or across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed, not gripping the seat. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you catch yourself bracing with it; also stop if you feel sharp pain at the front of the knee.
dose: 3 × 10–15, RIR 2–3 (1–2 from Phase 1 week 4), 1-s squeeze, 2–3-s lowering

name: Hamstring curl (seated machine preferred)
why: Strong hamstrings balance your quads, protect your knees and control your stride on descents. The seated curl trains them through a long range with your back supported, and you can get in and out with one hand.
setup: Use the seated version if your gym has both; the lying version means getting on and off face down.
Adjust the backrest so your knees line up with the machine's pivot.
Set the lower pad on the back of your lower calves, just above the heels.
Lower the thigh pad onto your thighs with your uninjured hand so your legs are pinned snugly.
Sit tall, uninjured hand on the handle, injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Pull your heels down and back under the seat
Squeeze for 1 s at the end of the curl
Return for 3 s until your legs are nearly straight
Hips and back stay still against the pad
Breathe out as you curl
mistakes: Lifting the hips or arching to finish a rep: lighten the load and tighten the thigh pad.
Cutting the range short: let the legs straighten almost fully, under control, every rep.
Letting the stack slam down: slow, 3-second returns.
arm_safety: Seated curl: sit down using your legs, put your heels on the pad, then lower the thigh pad with your uninjured hand (ask staff if the lever needs two hands); to get out, lift the thigh pad with your uninjured hand, slide your legs out and stand using your legs. Lying curl: kneel onto the pad from the foot end, then lower your chest onto it with your uninjured hand on the front handle; to get off, slide backwards feet-first until your feet reach the floor, then stand up. Never press up through your injured arm or rest your head on it. Arm: across your stomach when seated, or resting on the pad beside your head when lying (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you catch yourself bracing with it.
dose: 3 × 8–12, RIR 2–3 (1–2 from Phase 1 week 4), 3-s lowering

name: Box squat (bodyweight)
equipment: bench or box about knee height
why: The squat is the most functional pattern you own: standing up from a chair, from the floor, from a rest on a hillside. Squatting to a box teaches you to sit back with control, Pavel-style crisp and braced, and gives you a safe seat behind you while you build depth and confidence without holding anything.
setup: Back a bench or knee-height box against a wall or rack so it can't slide.
Stand with your heels about a foot's length in front of it, feet shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly.
Injured arm across your stomach; reach your uninjured arm forward at shoulder height as a counterbalance.
Breathe into your belly and brace lightly, about a third of your maximum, never a full breath-hold strain.
cues: Sit back and down; reach your bottom towards the box
Knees follow your toes; whole foot planted
Touch the box lightly and pause 1 s; don't flop
Stand by pushing the floor away and breathe out on the way up
Chest proud, eyes forward
mistakes: Dropping onto the box: slow the last third, touch softly, then pause.
Rocking back and using momentum to stand: keep your weight over mid-foot and lean forward slightly to start the rise.
Knees caving in on the way up: think 'knees out' and widen your stance a little.
arm_safety: No hands needed at any point: you sit and stand with your legs. Keep your injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one) and use only your uninjured arm as a counterbalance. The box behind you means a loss of balance ends with you sitting down rather than falling, so make sure it is stable and backed against something. Never reach back to the box with either hand. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady.
dose: 10 easy reps as your leg-press ramp-up in Phases 0–1; or 3 × 15–20 with a 4-s lowering when the leg press is busy

name: Tempo squat (bodyweight)
equipment: bench or box (depth guide and safety seat)
why: Slowing the squat right down (3 seconds down, a pause, then up) makes bodyweight hard enough to build muscle and teaches the control you need on steep descents. In your plan it's also the circuit station that stands in for the sled drag, and it's the bridge to loaded squats after clearance.
setup: Stand in front of a bench or box backed against a wall or rack, as a depth guide and safety seat.
Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out; injured arm across your stomach, uninjured arm reaching forward.
Light brace. Tempo: 3 s down, 1 s hover just above the box, 1–2 s up.
cues: Count '3-2-1' on the way down
Hover just above the box for 1 s and stay tight
Drive up smoothly and breathe out
Heels down, knees over toes
mistakes: Speeding up halfway down: count out loud and slow the bottom third.
Resting on the box instead of hovering: if you can't hover, touch lightly and use a higher box.
Holding your breath during the slow descent: breathe in at the top and out on the way up; small breaths in the pause are fine.
arm_safety: No hands needed. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one); uninjured arm forward as a counterbalance only. The box stays behind you so a loss of balance ends with a sit, not a fall; keep it backed against a wall or rack. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady.
dose: 3 × 15–25, tempo 3-1-1, RIR 2–3 (circuit station: 10–12 reps, 3 s down)

name: Wall sit
why: A simple isometric hold that builds the quad endurance you need for hours of hill walking, and many people find holds like this kind to their knees. It's also one of your progress tests.
setup: Stand with your back flat against a smooth wall, feet hip-width and about 40–60 cm out from it.
Injured arm across your stomach; uninjured hand resting by your side.
Slide down until your knees are bent to about 60° (a shallow sit) at first; build towards 90°, thighs parallel to the floor, over the weeks.
cues: Back and head against the wall
Knees over your ankles, not past your toes
Weight through your heels and mid-foot
Slow, steady breathing the whole time
mistakes: Pushing your hands on your thighs to make it easier: keep both arms off your legs.
Holding your breath: you should be able to count out loud throughout.
Knees drifting inwards: push them gently out in line with your toes.
arm_safety: No hands needed. To finish, slide back up the wall by pushing through your legs, or walk your feet back towards the wall first; don't push off your thighs with either hand. Use a smooth wall and a grippy floor so your feet can't slide. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel sharp knee pain.
dose: 3–5 × 30–45 s holds, 60 s rest (test: one maximum hold every 4 weeks)

name: Spanish squat (heavy band)
equipment: heavy loop band (bring your own if the gym has none)
squat rack upright or sturdy post
bench or box as a backstop
why: A heavy band behind your knees lets you sit back with upright shins, putting a big load on the quads with little stress on the knee joint. It's a knee-friendly way to build the quad strength that makes long descents comfortable.
setup: Loop a thick, heavy band around a rack upright or sturdy post at knee height, using your uninjured hand.
Step both legs into the loop and lift it so it sits behind your knees, at the top of the calves.
Walk backwards until the band is tight; feet hip-width, toes facing the anchor.
Place a bench or box behind you as a backstop in case the band slips.
Injured arm across your stomach; uninjured arm forward.
cues: Sit back into the band like a reverse wall sit
Shins stay vertical and your torso stays upright
Go as deep as you can control, then hold
Breathe steadily throughout the hold
mistakes: Hinging forward at the hips: stay tall so the load stays on the quads.
Band too low on the calves or too high on the thighs: keep it right behind the knee crease.
Not enough tension: step back further so you can really sit into it.
arm_safety: Set up and take down the band with your uninjured hand only. To finish, stand up tall, step forward to take the tension off, then step out one leg at a time. If the band slips or snaps you would sit backwards, so always have a bench or box behind you and check the band for nicks before each use. No heavy band? Do wall sits instead. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel sharp knee pain. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 4–5 × 30–45 s holds, 60–90 s rest

name: Split squat (bodyweight, supported)
equipment: squat rack upright or wall for your uninjured hand
why: Every step up a hill is a mini split squat. This builds single-leg strength and hip control in a long, stable stance, and it's the foundation for the loaded split squats that come after clearance.
setup: Stand side-on to a rack upright or wall with your uninjured hand resting on it.
Take a long step: front foot flat, back foot on the ball of the foot, feet hip-width apart (like standing on train tracks, not a tightrope).
Optional: a folded mat under the back knee.
Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Drop the back knee straight down towards the floor
Front knee travels forward over the toes; front heel stays down
Torso tall or very slightly forward
Push up through the front foot and breathe out
mistakes: Stance too narrow, so you wobble: widen your feet to hip-width.
Pushing off the back leg: keep most of your weight on the front foot.
Front knee caving in: slow down and keep it over the middle toes.
arm_safety: Your uninjured hand stays on the support for the whole set: a light touch for balance, not a pull. Switch legs by swapping which foot is in front; stay side-on so the support stays by your uninjured hand. Step out of the stance slowly by bringing the back foot forward. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3 × 12–20 per leg, RIR 2–3, 3-s lowering

name: Rear-foot-elevated split squat (bodyweight, supported)
equipment: squat rack upright for your uninjured hand
why: One of the best single-leg builders there is: it loads the front leg hard with bodyweight alone and stretches the back hip, which helps your stride on long walks. It's the bodyweight version of the Bulgarian split squat you'll load after clearance.
setup: Put a bench right next to a rack upright, with the upright on your uninjured side so you can hold it throughout. A lower step is easier than a full-height bench.
Stand in front of the bench, facing away from it, uninjured hand on the upright.
Reach one foot back and rest the top of that foot (laces down) on the bench.
Shuffle (never hop) the front foot forward until your front shin is roughly vertical to slightly forward at the bottom. Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Lower straight down, back knee towards the floor
Most of your weight on the front heel and mid-foot
A slight forward lean from the hips is fine
Control 2–3 s down, drive up through the front foot, breathe out
mistakes: Front foot too close, so the heel lifts: move it further forward.
Bouncing off the back foot: the back leg is a kickstand only.
Wobbling sideways: widen your stance and keep your uninjured hand on the upright.
arm_safety: Getting in and out is the risky part. Always put your uninjured hand on the upright before you lift the back foot onto the bench. To finish, stand tall, shift all your weight onto the front foot, lift the back foot off the bench and step it down, then rest. Facing the same way for both legs keeps the upright by your uninjured hand. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3 × 10–15 per leg, RIR 2–3, 3-s lowering and a 1-s pause

name: Step-up (bodyweight)
equipment: aerobic step (15–25 cm) or the bottom stair until full clearance; never a bench before then
rack upright, wall or banister for your uninjured hand
why: The single most specific hiking exercise: it is walking uphill. It builds each leg on its own and teaches you to drive up without pushing off the back foot, and the slow step down trains your descents too.
setup: Until full clearance: an aerobic step (15–25 cm) backed against a wall or rack so it can't slide, or the bottom stair with the banister on your uninjured side. Start low and build to the step's top height; boxes up to knee height wait for full clearance, and a bench is never your step before then.
No aerobic step at the gym? Use the bottom stair at home with your uninjured hand on the banister.
Stand facing the box with a wall or rack upright within reach of your uninjured hand.
Place your whole working foot on the box. Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Lean forward slightly and drive up through the whole top foot
Don't spring off the bottom foot; let it go light
Stand fully tall at the top
Step down slowly (3 s) with the same leg doing the work
Breathe out as you rise
mistakes: Only the toes on the box: get your whole foot on, heel included.
Bouncing off the floor leg: pause the floor foot on its toes before each rep.
Knee caving inwards: use a lower step and keep the knee over the middle toes.
Dropping down fast: control the descent, because that's half the hiking benefit.
arm_safety: No hands needed for the movement; your uninjured hand touches or hovers by the wall or upright at all times. Catching a toe on the box edge is the main fall risk, so lift your foot clearly, start low and never rush. Do all reps on one leg, then the other, rather than alternating quickly. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3 × 12–20 per leg, RIR 2–3, 3-s lowering (circuit: 8 per leg on the aerobic step)

name: Lateral step-up (bodyweight)
equipment: aerobic step (15–25 cm) or the bottom stair until full clearance
why: Trails make you step sideways around rocks, roots and stiles. Stepping up from the side trains knee control and the side-hip muscles that stop your knee collapsing when the ground is uneven.
setup: Put an aerobic step (15–25 cm) against a wall. Stand beside it facing the wall, so your uninjured hand can rest on the wall.
Place the near foot on the box; the other foot is on the floor beside it.
Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Push down through the whole foot on the box to lift yourself
Knee tracks over the middle toes; no caving in
Hips stay level at the top
Lower the floor foot slowly (3 s) and just tap the floor
Breathe out as you rise
mistakes: Pushing off the floor foot: keep it light, a tap only.
Hip hiking (one side shooting up): use a lower step height and stand tall.
Knee diving inwards: slow down and use a lower step height.
arm_safety: Facing the wall means your uninjured hand can rest on it for both legs: for the other leg, move to the other side of the box and keep facing the wall. Uninjured hand touching or hovering by the wall throughout. Step on and off the box deliberately, never in a hurry. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3 × 12–15 per leg, RIR 2–3

name: Eccentric step-down (to the side)
equipment: aerobic step (15–25 cm) until full clearance; higher boxes only after it
wall or rack upright for your uninjured hand
why: Descents, not climbs, are what tire and irritate knees on long hikes. Slowly lowering yourself on one leg trains exactly that braking strength and knee control, so your quads protect your joints late in the day.
setup: Place an aerobic step against a wall (its lowest height, about 15 cm, to start; up to 25 cm before full clearance), and stand on it facing the wall with your uninjured hand resting on it.
Stand on the working leg near the side edge and let the other leg hang off the side.
Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Hips back slightly, chest a little forward
Lower for 3–4 s until the free heel lightly taps the floor
Knee stays over the middle toes
Tap, don't transfer your weight
Breathe steadily
mistakes: Dropping the last few centimetres: use a lower step height until you can control the whole way.
Knee collapsing inwards: slow down and aim the knee over your little toe side.
Putting weight onto the floor foot: just kiss the floor and come back up, or step up with both legs if you can't rise on one yet.
arm_safety: Uninjured hand on the wall or upright throughout. If you can't stand back up on one leg yet, put both feet on the floor and step back onto the box with your uninjured hand still on the support; that keeps it pure lowering work. For the other leg, stand on the other foot and let the free leg hang off the other side, still facing the wall. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3 × 8–12 per leg, 3–4-s lowering, RIR 2–3

name: Patrick step
equipment: aerobic step at its lowest height (about 15 cm) or the bottom stair: not a stack of plates or a bench
wall or rack upright for your uninjured hand
muscles: quads (especially the inner quad near the knee)
why: Popularised by Ben Patrick (Knees Over Toes / ATG), this trains your knee to travel forward over your toes under control, which is exactly what happens on every steep downhill step. It builds knee tolerance and inner-quad strength with bodyweight only.
setup: Stand on the aerobic step (lowest height, about 15 cm) next to a wall or rack upright on your uninjured side.
Stand on the working leg and let the other leg hang straight in front of the step, heel just off the floor.
Later progression (after full clearance): raise the working heel slightly on a slant board.
Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Let the working knee travel forward over your toes
Lower until the front heel lightly taps the floor
Front leg stays straight; torso upright
Rise by straightening the working knee, slow and smooth
Breathe steadily
mistakes: Sitting the hips back instead of driving the knee forward: think 'knee over toes'.
Working heel lifting off the step: let the knee go less far.
Bending the front leg to reach the floor: keep it straight and shorten the range if needed.
arm_safety: Uninjured hand touching or hovering by the support for every rep. You face the same way for both legs, so the support stays on your uninjured side; just swap which foot stands on the step. The step must be solid and non-slip. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, you feel unsteady, or you get sharp pain at the front of the knee (a muscle burn is normal). Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 2–3 × 12–15 per leg, slow and controlled

name: Box pistol (single-leg squat to a box)
equipment: squat rack upright for your uninjured hand
why: Standing up from a low seat on one leg is a real-world strength test, and it builds the single-leg drive you need for big steps up rocky paths. It's the most demanding leg exercise in this part of your library, so it comes after your step-downs are solid.
setup: Place a bench or box against a rack upright, with the upright on your uninjured side. Start high: knee height or above (a bench plus a folded mat, or a tall box).
Stand on one leg in front of the box, heel about a foot's length away, uninjured hand holding the upright.
Hold the free leg slightly in front of you, heel just off the floor. Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Sit back and down to the box over 3 s
Touch the box lightly and stay tall; don't flop
Lean forward from the hips, then stand up through the whole foot
Knee tracks over the middle toes
Breathe out as you stand
mistakes: Falling back onto the box at the end: use a higher box until you control the whole descent.
Rocking and swinging to stand: pause on the box, lean forward, then drive up.
Pulling hard on the upright: the hand is for balance; if you need to pull, the box is too low.
arm_safety: Locked until full clearance: this is the highest balance demand in your library, and a fall onto a healing forearm is the biggest risk you have. When cleared: This is the highest balance demand in your Part A library. Always hold the upright with your uninjured hand, always have the box behind you, and never reach back with either hand. If you lose balance, sit down onto the box and put both feet down rather than trying to save the rep. Only lower the box when every rep at the current height is smooth. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 2–3 × 3–6 per leg, RIR 2–3

name: Single-leg Romanian deadlift (bodyweight, supported)
equipment: squat rack upright or wall for your uninjured hand
why: Trains your hamstrings and glutes one side at a time while teaching your ankle, knee and hip to balance together: the terrain-proofing you need on uneven ground. It also grooves the hip hinge you'll later load for deadlifts and carries.
setup: Stand side-on to a rack upright or wall with your uninjured hand resting on it.
Stand on the working leg with a soft knee (about 15–20° bend).
Injured arm across your stomach.
Easier version: keep the back toes lightly on the floor behind you as a kickstand.
cues: Push your hips back as the free leg reaches back
Body and back leg move as one straight line, like a see-saw
Hips stay square to the floor; don't open up
Go until you feel a hamstring stretch or your torso is near parallel
Drive the hip forward to stand and breathe out
mistakes: Rounding your back to reach lower: stop where your back is still flat.

Put the free foot down between reps whenever you feel wobbly. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.

Lower slowly

Hamstring cramping: bring the planted heel a little closer and push through the whole heel.

arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. Feet too far from your bottom: bring them closer for a more stable base.

Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. equipment: flat bench backed against a wall or rack

Get into position without your arms (see arm safety): upper back on the bench edge, just below the shoulder blades.

Injured arm across your stomach; uninjured arm resting along the bench or across your chest.

Ribs down, slight pelvic tuck

Squeeze your glutes for 2 s
Lower under control; breathe out as you lift

Bench sliding away: always back it against a wall or rack.

(Or get down to the floor via kneeling with your uninjured hand on the bench, then sit with your back to it.) Drive through the planted heel to a flat tabletop
Hips stay level; no twisting
2 s squeeze at the top, 2–3 s down
Breathe out as you lift

Over-arching to finish: stop at a straight hip and tuck the pelvis.
Bench sliding: always back it against something solid.

To finish, lower your hips to the floor, roll onto your uninjured side and come up via kneeling with your uninjured hand on the bench. Never push on the bench or floor with your injured arm. Arm: across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

Small range, big squeeze, 1 s hold
Return slowly over 2–3 s
Breathe out as you kick back

Twisting the hip open: keep the toes pointing at the floor.
Gripping the frame hard: a light touch only; if you need to pull, the weight is too heavy.

Uninjured hand on the frame for balance throughout; facing the machine works for both legs. Unclip the cable before removing the strap, and step away only when the weight is resting on the stack. No ankle strap? Do single-leg glute bridges instead. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). name: Cable hip abduction (ankle strap)

Lift the leg out to the side, leading with the heel, toes forward
Small range (about 30°), 1 s pause
Return slowly over 2–3 s
Breathe out as you lift
mistakes: Leaning the whole body sideways: lighter weight, smaller range, stand tall.
Toes turning up and the leg drifting forward: keep the toes pointing forward.
Letting the stack yank the leg back in: control the return.

When the strapped leg is on your injured side, your uninjured hand is the one nearest the machine, which is easy. For the other leg, turn round and reach your uninjured hand across your body to the frame (or hold a separate upright), and keep the weight light, because the cable pulls you sideways. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady.

name: Cable hip adduction (ankle strap)
equipment: cable machine with an ankle strap (not every gym has one)

Sweep the strapped leg across in front of your standing leg

Hips stay square; no twisting
Breathe out as you pull in

Standing too close, so there's no tension at the start: step away until the leg starts about 20–30° out.
Leaning towards the machine: stand tall.

For the other leg, turn round and reach your uninjured hand across to the frame (or hold a separate upright), and keep the weight light, because the cable pulls you towards the machine. No ankle strap? Do side-lying hip adduction instead. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady.

Lie on your side with the bottom knee bent for stability and the top leg straight, in line with your body.

Don't let the top hip roll backwards
Breathe normally

Lifting too high and side-bending: smaller range, stay stacked.

Leg on your uninjured side: the default is standing, facing the rack with your uninjured hand on the upright, lifting the leg out to the side with a 2-s hold (15–20 reps). Getting down and up: kneel with only your uninjured hand on the bench and roll onto your uninjured side to sit up, never pushing through the injured arm. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

name: Side-lying hip adduction
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: A simple, safe way to strengthen your inner thighs, which steady your knees and pelvis on side-slopes and uneven ground. It needs nothing but a mat.

Lie on your side with the bottom leg straight.
Bend the top leg and place that foot flat on the floor in front of the bottom knee.
Rest your head on a folded towel, not on your arm.

Bottom leg straight, toes pointing forward
Pause 1–2 s at the top
Lower slowly over 3 s
Breathe normally

Swinging the leg: slow, controlled lifts with a pause.
Toes turning up to the ceiling: keep them pointing forward.

Training the other leg means lying on your injured side: only if your clinic is happy with it and it's comfortable (upper arm takes the contact, forearm on a towel in front of you, nothing on it). Your plan uses the adductor-squeeze bridge instead, which trains both sides lying on your back. Get down and up via a bench with your uninjured hand and roll onto your uninjured side to sit up. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

name: 45° back extension (hip-hinge style)
equipment: 45° back extension bench (not every gym has one; alternative: bench hip thrust)
why: Builds the back of your body (glutes, hamstrings and the muscles along your spine) that keeps you upright under a rucksack for hours and makes you robust for lifting and carrying later.
setup: Set the hip pad so its top edge sits just below your hip bones, letting you hinge freely (ask staff if the adjustment needs two hands).
Step onto the footplate one foot at a time with your uninjured hand on the handle; heels against the ankle rollers.
Lean into the pad and fold your arms: injured arm resting across your chest, uninjured forearm over it.

Lower until you feel a hamstring stretch
Squeeze your glutes to come up to a straight line; pause 1–2 s
Don't overarch at the top
Breathe out as you rise
mistakes: Over-arching the lower back at the top: stop at a straight line from head to heels.
Rounding and un-rounding the spine: keep your back neutral and move at the hips.
Pad too high to hinge: lower it so your hips are free.

Getting off: come up to a straight line, take the handle with your uninjured hand and step down one foot at a time. Arm: resting across your chest under your uninjured forearm (or in its sling if you still wear one); never reach for the floor or a handle with it. No 45° bench at your gym? Do bench hip thrusts instead. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady getting on or off. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.

name: Sled drag forwards (waist belt or harness)
equipment: waist belt or a dip belt with a chain, clipped to the sled strap (many gyms have no sled belt)
why: Strength as cardio: walking against a loaded sled builds leg drive and work capacity, much like climbing with a pack. It's almost all pushing with very little lowering, so it causes little soreness and you recover quickly, and with a belt your hands stay completely free. Many gyms have no sled belt, so your plan uses tempo squats until you get one.

Put the belt on with your uninjured hand, attachment point at your back.
Check the lane in front of you is clear for at least 20 m.
Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling); uninjured arm swings naturally.

Short, powerful steps; push the floor behind you
Steady walking pace; never run
Breathe rhythmically; you should manage a short sentence
Stop before your form breaks
mistakes: Too heavy, so you stomp and strain: lighten it until you can walk steadily.
Jerking the sled from a standstill: take up the slack slowly before your first step.
Bending at the waist: lean from the ankles with your chest up.

Staff load the plates (after good-arm clearance you may load small plates one at a time with your uninjured hand); clip the strap on with your uninjured hand. To stop, walk the tension off and stand still before turning round. Flat, dry turf with a clear lane only, and no sprinting. If the strap snags or the sled jams, stop and step back to slacken it rather than lunging forward. No belt? Your plan uses tempo squats in its place. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

name: Sled drag backwards (waist belt)
equipment: waist belt or a dip belt with a chain, clipped to the sled strap (many gyms have no sled belt)
why: Walking backwards against a sled works the quads around the knee hard with little stress on the joint and very little soreness. Knee-focused coaches such as the Knees Over Toes Guy use it to bulletproof knees, which is exactly what you want for downhill hiking, and it's excellent conditioning too. Many gyms have no sled belt, so your plan uses tempo squats until you get one.

Ask staff to attach and load the sled; start with the empty sled.
Face the sled, step back until the strap is taut, and look over your shoulder to check the lane behind you is completely clear.
Injured arm across your stomach; uninjured arm relaxed.

Small steps back, pushing through the balls of your feet
Let your knees travel forward over your toes
Steady pace; glance back every few steps
Breathe rhythmically
mistakes: Big, reaching steps: keep them short and quick.
Standing up tall, which takes the work off the quads: stay in a slight squat.
Never checking behind you: glance back regularly, because that's where the fall risk is.

Walking backwards is the main risk: use only a flat, dry, empty lane, ask someone to watch your path if the gym is busy, and keep the pace slow. Legs straight, weight on your heels.

Pause 1 s at the top
Lower slowly; don't slap your feet down
Keep your bottom against the wall
Walk your feet further out to make it harder

Bending the knees to cheat: keep your legs straight.

To finish, walk your feet back towards the wall in small steps before standing away from it; don't push off with your hands. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

Lie on your back and lift your knees over your hips, knees bent at 90° (the tabletop).

Breathe out fully and gently flatten your lower back towards the mat.

Slowly lower one heel to tap the floor (3 s), then bring it back

Holding your breath: exhale slowly on every rep.
