arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 3 × 6–8 per side, slow

name: Tuck hollow hold
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: A gymnastics staple that teaches tension through the whole front of your core: the stiffness that protects your back when you carry and lift later. The tucked version is arm-free and easy to scale: straighten one leg, then both, as it gets easy.
setup: Get down onto a mat next to a bench (see arm safety).
Lie on your back with your knees bent and pulled up towards your chest (hips past 90°).
Arms long by your sides on the mat; your injured arm simply rests there, not pressing (or keep it across your stomach).
Breathe out and press your lower back into the mat.
cues: Lift your head and shoulder blades just off the mat, chin slightly tucked
Lower back stays glued to the floor
Short, steady breaths behind a light brace
Progress: one leg out, then both legs out at about 45°
mistakes: Neck straining: look at your knees, tuck your chin and lower your shoulders a little.
Lower back lifting: tuck the knees closer to your chest.
Holding your breath: keep breathing; if you can't, the hold is too hard.
arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: resting by your side or across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), never pushing into the floor. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

name: Reverse crunch
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: Trains your abs to curl the pelvis, the control you use to lift your legs over stiles and rocks, and lays the foundation for hanging knee raises after full clearance.
setup: Get down onto a mat next to a bench (see arm safety).
Lie on your back with your knees bent at 90° over your hips.
Uninjured hand flat on the mat by your side; injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Breathe out and curl your hips off the mat, knees towards your chest
Think 'roll the tailbone up', not 'swing the legs'
Pause 1 s at the top
Lower your hips slowly over 3 s
Head and shoulders stay relaxed on the mat
mistakes: Swinging the legs for momentum: smaller, slower curls.
Pushing hard through the hand: your abs do the work; the hand only rests.
Dropping back down fast: 3-second lowering every rep.
arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), hand relaxed. Keep the curl small so you don't roll towards your injured side. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.

name: McGill curl-up
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: One of Prof. Stuart McGill's 'Big 3': it trains the front of your core to hold your spine steady without the repeated bending of a sit-up. That spinal stiffness is what protects your back under a pack or a heavy carry.
setup: Get down onto a mat next to a bench (see arm safety).
Lie on your back with one knee bent (foot flat) and the other leg straight.
Slide your uninjured hand, palm down, under your lower back, or use a small folded towel, to keep its natural arch.
Injured arm resting across your chest.
cues: Brace lightly, as if expecting a poke in the stomach
Lift only your head and shoulders a few centimetres, as one unit; no chin-poke
Hold for 8–10 s, breathing steadily
Your lower back doesn't move at all
Swap the bent leg halfway through
mistakes: Curling up high like a crunch: a few centimetres is enough.
Flattening or rounding the lower back: keep the arch over your hand or towel.
Holding your breath: take short breaths throughout the hold.
arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: resting across your chest (or in its sling if you still wear one); only your uninjured hand or the towel goes under your back. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 3 × 5 holds of 8–10 s, 45 s rest (or McGill's 5-3-1 descending pyramid); add reps, not longer holds

name: Single-leg balance (supported)
why: Better balance is your best protection against the fall you most need to avoid, and it's the base of moving well on uneven ground. A few minutes a day trains the reflexes in your ankles and hips.
setup: Stand facing a wall at arm's length with the fingertips of your uninjured hand touching it.
Firm, flat, non-slip floor; trainers on.
Injured arm across your stomach.
Lift one foot a few centimetres, with a slight bend in the standing knee.
cues: Hips level; don't sink into the standing hip
Spread your weight across your whole foot
Eyes on a fixed point at eye level
Fingertips ready, not leaning
Progress: fingertips hovering, then slow head turns, then free-leg reaches; eyes-closed work waits for full clearance
mistakes: Leaning on the wall: fingertip contact only.
Locking the standing knee: keep a soft bend.
Progressing too fast: remove support only when 30 s is easy, and keep eyes-closed work for after full clearance, fingertips on the wall.
arm_safety: This exercise is meant to challenge your balance, so the support is non-negotiable before full clearance: your uninjured hand stays touching, or within a few centimetres of, the wall, and you put the lifted foot down the moment you wobble. No wobble boards, balance boards or foam pads until you're fully cleared. Facing the wall works for both legs. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 30 s per leg every day in your mobility routine; 45–60 s holds as a test

name: 90/90 breathing
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: Teaches you to breathe low and wide and to exhale fully: the foundation for bracing without straining (no breath-holding while your bone heals) and for staying relaxed at Zone 2. It also helps you switch off after training.
setup: Get down onto a mat next to a wall or bench (see arm safety).
Lie on your back with your feet flat on the wall, or calves resting on a bench, so your hips and knees are at 90°.
Press your heels gently into the wall until you feel the backs of your thighs switch on and your lower back settle towards the mat.
Injured arm resting across your stomach; uninjured hand on your lower ribs.
cues: Breathe in through your nose for about 4 s; feel your belly, sides and back widen
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6–8 s and let your ribs drop
At the end of the out-breath, pause for 2–3 relaxed seconds
Shoulders and neck stay soft
mistakes: Breathing into your chest and shoulders: think 'widen the lower ribs'.
Forcing the out-breath until you strain: long and gentle, never a breath-hold strain.
Arching your lower back: press your heels into the wall a little more.
arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down, sit to one side, then lower yourself onto your back by leaning on your uninjured elbow. Getting up: bend your knees, roll onto your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand to side-sitting, come up to kneeling, put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Never roll onto, lean on or push through your injured arm. Arm: resting across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). If you feel light-headed, breathe normally and sit up slowly via your uninjured side. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 5 slow breaths (1–2 rounds)

name: Knee-to-wall ankle mobilisation
why: Ankle bend (dorsiflexion) lets your knee travel forward on steep climbs, descents and deep squats. Stiff ankles push the strain up into your knees and hips, which is why this is in your daily routine.
setup: Stand facing a wall in a short split stance, front toes about 5–10 cm from the wall.
Uninjured hand flat on the wall at chest height; injured arm across your stomach.
Back leg relaxed, toes on the floor.
cues: Drive the front knee forward towards the wall, over your second and third toes
Front heel stays glued to the floor
Touch the wall lightly, then back off
When it's easy, slide the foot back 1 cm
Smooth rocks; breathe normally
mistakes: Heel lifting: move the foot closer to the wall.
Knee caving inwards: aim the knee at the middle of your foot.
Bouncing: smooth rocks with a 1–2 s hold at the end.
arm_safety: Both feet stay down and your uninjured hand is on the wall, so the balance demand is minimal. Facing the wall works for both legs. Don't lean into the wall with your injured arm; keep it across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel a pinch at the front of the ankle (back off the range).
dose: 10 rocks per side (test: note your furthest toe-to-wall distance every 4 weeks)

name: 90/90 hip switches
equipment: bench nearby (for getting down and up)
why: Moves both hips through internal and external rotation, the twisting range your hips need on uneven ground and over stiles. Healthy hip rotation also takes strain off your knees and lower back.
setup: Get down onto a mat next to a bench (see arm safety).
Sit on the mat, knees bent about 90°, feet flat and wider than your hips.
Uninjured hand on the mat behind you for support; injured arm resting in your lap.
cues: Let both knees fall to one side so each leg makes a 90° angle
Sit tall over the front shin
Lift the knees and rotate them through to the other side
Move slowly and breathe out as you switch
Progress to doing it hands-free
mistakes: Slumping: sit tall, leaning back onto your uninjured hand as much as you need.
Forcing the range: go only as far as is comfortable; it improves with practice.
Feet too close together: widen them.
arm_safety: Getting down: stand beside a bench with your uninjured hand on it, step one foot back and lower that knee onto the mat, bring the other knee down and sit to one side. Getting up: turn onto your knees on your uninjured side, push up with your uninjured hand, then put your uninjured hand on the bench and stand up one leg at a time. Only your uninjured hand ever supports you on the floor; if you tip, sit back onto your uninjured hand rather than putting your injured hand down. Arm: resting in your lap (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel a pinch in the hip.
dose: 8 switches (4 each way)

name: Couch stretch (bench-supported)
equipment: thick mat or pad for the knee
rack upright or second bench for your uninjured hand
why: Opens the front of the hip and thigh, which tighten with sitting and get worked hard by miles of walking. Freer hip flexors let your glutes drive each stride and ease pressure on your lower back.
setup: Place a thick folded mat on the floor right in front of a bench, with a rack upright or a second bench within reach of your uninjured hand.
Uninjured hand on the support. Kneel on the mat with one knee close to the bench.
Place the top of that foot (laces down) on the bench behind you.
Step the other foot forward into a lunge, foot flat. Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Tuck your pelvis under and squeeze the glute of the back leg
Bring your torso upright only as far as you can keep the tuck
Breathe slowly and let the stretch build
Feel it at the front of the back thigh and hip, not in the knee
mistakes: Arching your lower back to get upright: keep the tuck, even if you stay leaning forward.
Knee pressure on a hard floor: use a thick pad.
Back knee too close to the bench, so the stretch is too intense: start further away and edge closer over the weeks.
arm_safety: Unlocks at Light use / rehab started; until then the half-kneeling hip flexor stretch is the last stretch in your daily routine. Getting in and out is the risky moment, so your uninjured hand stays on the support throughout. To get out, lean forward over the front leg, slide the back foot off the bench to the floor, then stand up through a half-kneel with your uninjured hand on the support. Face the same way for both legs so the support stays on your uninjured side. Your injured hand never goes on the floor or bench; keep the arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady or sharp knee pain. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 45 s per side (1–2 rounds), from Light use / rehab started; until then the half-kneeling hip flexor stretch

name: Deep squat hold (to a box)
equipment: low box, step or bench as a safety seat
rack upright for your uninjured hand
why: Being able to sit comfortably at the bottom of a squat keeps your hips, knees and ankles healthy, and it's how you'll get down to tie a boot or rest on a hillside. The box behind you makes it safe.
setup: Place a low box or step (about 20–30 cm) behind you, close to a rack upright.
Feet shoulder-width or a little wider, toes turned out 15–30°.
Hold the upright lightly with your uninjured hand at about chest height as a counterbalance; injured arm across your stomach.
Slowly sit down as deep as you can, with the box ready to catch you.
cues: Heels down (small plates under them if they lift)
Knees out over your toes
Chest tall; let your hips sink
Breathe slowly and relax into it
Shift gently side to side to explore the position
mistakes: Collapsing into a deep slump: use a light hold on the upright to stay tall.
Heels lifting: raise them slightly or widen your stance.
Forcing depth: if your hips or knees pinch, sit on the box and work at that height.
arm_safety: The box behind you means losing balance ends with a sit. Your uninjured hand holds the upright for balance and to help you rise; stand up by driving through your legs. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one); never reach down to the floor with it. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel a pinch in the hip or knee.
dose: 60 s total (build it up in 2–3 shorter holds if needed)

name: Standing hip circles (hip CARs)
why: Slow, controlled circles take each hip through its full range under muscle control, keeping it mobile for high steps, stiles and uneven ground, and your standing leg gets a balance workout too.
setup: Stand facing a wall or rack upright at arm's length, uninjured hand resting on it.
Stand tall on one leg with a soft knee; injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Lift the knee up in front to hip height
Open it out to the side as far as you can control
Turn the foot up and take the knee back behind you
Bring it down and through to the start, then reverse the direction
Pelvis and trunk stay still; only the hip moves
mistakes: Twisting the whole body: make the circle smaller and slower.
Rushing: each circle should take 5–10 s.
Leaning heavily on the support: light touch only.
arm_safety: Facing the support at arm's length gives the knee room to move and keeps your uninjured hand on it for both legs. Put the foot down whenever you wobble. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel a pinch in the hip.
dose: 5 slow circles each way per leg

name: Seated thoracic rotation
equipment: bench or sturdy chair without wheels
why: A mobile upper back lets you turn without twisting your lower back, which helps when looking around on the trail, reaching for things and, later, carrying. It also helps ease the upper-back stiffness that often comes with guarding an injured arm.
setup: Sit astride a bench (or on a sturdy chair), feet flat, knees about 90°.
Squeeze your knees against the bench to keep your hips still.
Rest your injured arm across your stomach and lay your uninjured forearm over it, or put your uninjured hand on your opposite shoulder.
cues: Sit tall first; grow through the top of your head
Turn your upper body to one side as far as is comfortable
Breathe out into the turn and hold 2–3 s
Hips and knees keep facing forward
Return to the centre and switch sides
mistakes: Moving the hips with the shoulders: squeeze your knees and keep your hips square.
Slumping: sit tall before every turn.
Yanking into the range: smooth, gentle turns.
arm_safety: Seated with both feet down, so balance risk is minimal. Keep your injured arm supported against your body so it moves with your trunk instead of swinging. Stand up from the bench using your legs. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 8 turns per side

name: Leg swings (supported)
why: A quick dynamic warm-up that loosens your hips in the directions you walk and step (forwards, backwards and sideways) before strength work or a long walk.
setup: Front-to-back: stand side-on to a wall or upright with your uninjured hand on it and swing the outside leg.
For the other leg, turn round and reach your uninjured hand across your body to the support.
Side-to-side: face the wall with your uninjured hand on it and swing one leg across in front of you and out to the side.
Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Stand tall on a soft standing knee
Start small and let the swing grow gradually
Relaxed, rhythmic swings; no kicking
Trunk stays still; the movement is at the hip
mistakes: Swinging hard from the first rep: build up over 5–6 swings.
Leaning back or rounding to get height: smaller swings, tall posture.
Letting go of the support: keep your uninjured hand on it throughout.
arm_safety: Your uninjured hand stays on the support for every swing; when you turn round for the other leg, reach it across your body. Keep the swings controlled so the momentum never pulls you off balance. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel unsteady.
dose: 10–15 swings each direction per leg

name: Wall calf stretch (straight and bent knee)
why: Your calves work hardest of all on hills and stairs. Stretching both calf muscles keeps the ankle range you need for climbing and descending and eases tightness after sessions.
setup: Stand facing a wall with your uninjured hand flat on it at shoulder height; injured arm across your stomach.
Step one leg back at least a foot's length, toes pointing forward, both heels flat.
Bend the front knee.
cues: Straight-knee version: back leg straight, move your hips towards the wall until you feel the calf
Bent-knee version: bend the back knee too, heel still down; you'll feel it lower in the calf
Hold 30 s and breathe slowly
Don't arch your back
mistakes: Back heel lifting: shorten your stance.
Toes turned out: point them forward or slightly in.
Bouncing: hold still and breathe.
arm_safety: Both feet stay on the floor and your uninjured hand is on the wall, so balance risk is minimal. Lean through your uninjured hand only; don't push your injured hand into the wall. Facing the wall works for both legs. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 2 × 30 s per leg, each version

name: Half-kneeling hip flexor stretch
equipment: bench or rack upright for your uninjured hand
why: A gentler version of the couch stretch that opens the front of the hip so your glutes can drive every stride. Good after long walks and stair-climber sessions.
setup: Put a pad on the floor beside a bench or rack upright, on your uninjured side.
Uninjured hand on the support; step one foot back and lower that knee onto the pad.
Front foot flat, front knee over the ankle. Injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Tuck your pelvis under (tail down) and squeeze the back-leg glute
Shift forward a few centimetres until you feel the front of the back hip
Stay tall; no arching
Hold and breathe slowly
mistakes: Arching your lower back and leaning forward: tuck the pelvis first, then shift.
Kneeling on a hard floor: always use a pad.
Pushing so far you feel it in the knee: a smaller shift and a bigger glute squeeze.
arm_safety: This is the last stretch in your daily routine; from Light use / rehab started the couch stretch can take its place. Kneel down and stand up through a half-kneel with your uninjured hand on the bench or upright, and face the same way for both legs so the support stays on your uninjured side. Your injured hand never goes to the floor. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 2 × 30–45 s per side (45 s per side in your daily routine)

name: Seated hamstring stretch on a bench
why: Keeps the backs of your thighs supple after hinges, hamstring curls and long walks, which helps your stride and your hip hinge. The seated version needs no balance at all.
setup: Sit sideways on a flat bench with one leg stretched along it, heel on the bench, knee soft.
Other foot flat on the floor beside the bench.
Uninjured hand on the bench beside you; injured arm resting in your lap.
cues: Sit tall, then hinge forward from your hips with a flat back
Stop when you feel a gentle stretch behind the thigh
Pull your toes back towards you to add the calf
Hold and breathe slowly; no bouncing
mistakes: Rounding your back to reach your toes: hinge from the hips; you don't need to touch anything.
Locking the knee hard: a small bend is fine.
Stretching into pain: mild tension only.
arm_safety: Seated, so balance risk is minimal. Swing the leg on and off the bench without using your injured arm, and stand up by pushing through your legs. A standing version (heel on a low step) is fine too, but only with your uninjured hand on a support. Injured arm in your lap or across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb.
dose: 2 × 30–45 s per leg

name: Stair climber (Zone 2)
why: The closest gym match to climbing a mountain: thousands of controlled step-ups that build your aerobic engine and leg endurance together. Done steadily in Zone 2, it's the backbone of your hiking fitness.
setup: Before you start, find the stop button and any safety clip; clip it to your clothing with your uninjured hand.
Step on while the stairs are stationary, uninjured hand on the rail.
Start at the slowest speed and build up gradually over 2–3 minutes.

Zone 2: 60–70% of your HRmax (HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age: about 187 for the 30-year-old example profile, so Zone 2 is about 112–131 bpm; the hub shows your numbers). Talk test: you can speak in full sentences but would rather not, and you could breathe through your nose. Rough cross-check: stay at or below 180 − age.
Settings: a slow speed at which you can place your whole foot on each step; for most people that's one of the lowest few levels.
cues: Stand tall; no leaning on or hanging from the rail
Whole foot on each step; push through the heel
Until full clearance: uninjured hand lightly on the rail, injured arm across your stomach
Steady rhythm and steady breathing
Slow the machine down rather than grabbing on when you tire
mistakes: Leaning on or gripping the rail (less work, worse posture): a light touch with your uninjured hand only; slow the speed until you can stand tall.
Tiptoeing on the front of each step: whole foot down every time.
Going too fast and drifting into Zone 3–4: check the talk test and your heart rate every few minutes.
arm_safety: Until full clearance: your uninjured hand rests lightly on the rail the whole time (a touch, not a lean), your injured arm stays across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), and the safety clip is on. Step on only while the stairs are stopped. Getting off: slow to the lowest speed, press stop, wait until the stairs stop completely, then step down carefully with your uninjured hand on the rail. Never step on or off moving stairs. After full clearance you can let go of the rail once you feel steady. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy, faint or unusually breathless. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: Tuesday engine: about 8–10 min in Zone 2 at first, building by 2–4 min a week to 30–35 min; uphill 4 × 4-min intervals from Phase 4

name: Incline treadmill walk
why: Walking uphill is exactly what you're training for. The incline treadmill gives you controllable, all-weather hill work in Zone 2 to build the aerobic base and leg endurance for long days in the hills.
setup: Stand on the stopped belt and clip the safety key to your clothing with your uninjured hand.
Start at the slowest speed and walk 3–5 min on the flat to warm up.
Raise the incline gradually: start around 3–6% and build towards 8–12% over the weeks, at about 4–5.5 km/h.

Zone 2: 60–70% of your HRmax (HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age: about 187 for the 30-year-old example profile, so Zone 2 is about 112–131 bpm; the hub shows your numbers). Talk test: full sentences are possible but you'd rather not, and you could breathe through your nose. Cross-check: at or below 180 − age.
cues: Until full clearance: uninjured hand lightly on the rail, injured arm across your stomach
Stand tall with a slight lean from the ankles, not the waist
Whole-foot contact; push through the heel and big toe
Stay in the middle of the belt
Use incline, not speed, to raise the effort
mistakes: Gripping or leaning on the rails: it takes much of the work away and changes your posture; keep a light touch with your uninjured hand and lower the incline until you can stand tall.
Leaning forward from the waist on steep grades: reduce the incline and stand tall.
Drifting to the back of the belt: stay near the front; look ahead, not down.
Stepping onto or off a moving belt: always start and stop with you standing on it.
arm_safety: The safety key is non-negotiable: clip it on before you start, so the belt stops if you drift back. Until full clearance: uninjured hand lightly on the rail throughout (a touch, not a lean), injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one), never holding anything. Start the belt at the slowest speed while you're standing on it; never step onto a moving belt. No phone scrolling and no turning round. To finish: lower the incline, slow to a stroll, press stop, wait for the belt to stop completely, then step off. After full clearance you can walk hands-free once you feel steady. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy, faint or unusually breathless.
dose: 20–60 min Zone 2

name: Upright exercise bike
why: Zero-impact, zero-balance cardio you can push safely: your warm-up every session, a Zone 2 option and, later, your harder interval sessions. It builds the engine for long hikes without pounding your legs.
setup: Use an upright stationary bike, not a spin bike you have to lean on. Adjust the seat with your uninjured hand before getting on, or ask staff.
Seat height: with your heel on the pedal at the bottom of the stroke, your leg is straight; with the ball of your foot on the pedal, the knee keeps a slight bend.
Sit tall. Uninjured hand resting lightly on the handlebar; injured arm across your stomach.

Zone 2: 60–70% of your HRmax (HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age: about 187 for the 30-year-old example profile, so Zone 2 is about 112–131 bpm; the hub shows your numbers). Talk test: full sentences but you'd rather not; nasal breathing possible. Cadence about 70–90 rpm with moderate resistance.
cues: Smooth circles; push and pull through the pedals
Knees track straight over your feet
Relaxed shoulders, tall chest
Adjust the resistance to stay in your zone
Breathe rhythmically
mistakes: Seat too low (ache at the front of the knee): raise it until the knee is just slightly bent at the bottom.
Seat too high (hips rocking side to side): lower it a notch.
Leaning on the handlebars: sit up; this bike needs no arm support.
arm_safety: Getting on: stand beside the bike with your uninjured hand on the handlebar, swing your leg over (or step through on a step-through frame) and sit. Getting off: stop pedalling completely, put one foot down, stand, and step away with your uninjured hand on the bar. Never lean on the bars with your injured arm; keep it across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy, faint or unusually breathless.
dose: 5 min easy as a warm-up; 20–45 min Zone 2

name: Recumbent bike
why: The most stable cardio option there is: a backrest, a low step-through seat and no need for your arms at all. Ideal for longer Zone 2 sessions, easy recovery days and amber-readiness days.
setup: Slide the seat (usually a lever under the seat, worked with your uninjured hand) so that at the furthest pedal position your knee is slightly bent.
Step through the frame and sit back into the backrest; slide your feet into the pedal straps.
Injured arm across your stomach; uninjured hand on the side handle if you like.

Zone 2: 60–70% of your HRmax (HRmax ≈ 208 − 0.7 × age: about 187 for the 30-year-old example profile, so Zone 2 is about 112–131 bpm; the hub shows your numbers). Talk test: full sentences but you'd rather not. Cadence about 70–90 rpm.
cues: Sit back with your lower back against the backrest
Smooth, even pedal strokes
Knees in line with your feet
Adjust the resistance to stay in your zone
mistakes: Seat too close (knees come up high, hips pinch): slide it back.
Seat too far (reaching with your toes): slide it forward.
Pedalling too easily for too long: add enough resistance to reach Zone 2.
arm_safety: Step-through frame: walk in, turn and sit down using your legs. Adjust the seat with your uninjured hand before you sit, or ask staff. To get off, stop pedalling, slide your feet out of the straps and stand up by pushing through your legs. Injured arm across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). If your gym has no recumbent bike, use the upright bike. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy, faint or unusually breathless.
dose: 20–60 min Zone 2

name: Outdoor walk (good paths)
equipment: supportive trainers or walking shoes with grip
why: You already walk; this turns it into training. Daily brisk walks build your aerobic base, your step count (towards 8,000–10,000 a day) and the tolerance in your feet and legs that long-distance hiking demands.
setup: Choose well-lit, even routes: pavements, parks, towpaths and surfaced tracks. Avoid ice, wet leaves, mud and dark, uneven ground until you're fully cleared.
Wear grippy, supportive shoes, carry your phone and water in a waist pack (2 kg or less) so your uninjured hand stays free, and wear something reflective on dark mornings.
Easy days: conversational pace. Zone 2 days: walk briskly or add gentle hills, so that you can speak in full sentences but would rather not (60–70% of HRmax; the hub shows your bpm).
cues: Tall posture, eyes ahead, not down at your phone
Quick, natural steps rather than long overstrides
Let your uninjured arm swing; injured arm relaxed
Push off through the big toe
Slow down on slopes, kerbs and wet patches
mistakes: Always walking at the same easy pace: include brisk Zone 2 sections and gentle hills.
Overstriding, with the heel slamming down in front: shorter, quicker steps.
Walking on risky surfaces to get the steps in: on icy or very wet days, walk on the treadmill instead.
arm_safety: Falls are the biggest risk while the bone heals, so route choice is your safety equipment: firm, even, well-lit paths only, and no ice or wet leaves. Keep your uninjured hand free (no coffee cup or phone in it) so it's ready for balance, and nothing in your injured hand or on that side's shoulder: a waist pack only until Light use / rehab started. If you still wear a sling, use it as instructed. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy or unusually breathless. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 30–60 min most days; build towards 8,000–10,000 steps a day

name: Outdoor hike (good paths first)
equipment: walking boots or trail shoes with grip
waist pack, 2 kg or less (water, snack, phone), until Light use / rehab started; a light day pack after that
why: This is the goal itself: long, steady days on your feet. Regular longer hikes build the endurance, foot toughness and pacing skills that no machine fully copies, on safe terrain until you're cleared for rougher ground.
setup: Until full clearance: hike Levels 1–3 only, as on the Hikes page: tarmac or firm, level gravel, dry, in daylight, on stile-free routes. No scrambling, scree, wet rock, mud, ice, steep descents or stiles.
Tell someone your route and return time, and carry a charged phone.

Carry it in a waist pack (2 kg or less), put on and taken off with your uninjured hand: nothing in your injured hand or on that side's shoulder. Pack walks with a day pack are the separate light-ruck exercise, from Light use / rehab started.
Pace in Zone 2: you can talk in full sentences but would rather not (60–70% of HRmax; the hub shows your bpm).
cues: Uphill: shorten your steps and keep a steady breathing rhythm; slow down rather than stop
Downhill: short steps, soft knees, eyes 2–3 steps ahead
Place your whole foot; avoid loose stones, roots and wet wood
Eat and drink a little every 45–60 min on longer outings
Turn back early if the path or the weather gets worse
mistakes: Starting too fast: the first 15 minutes should feel easy.
Long, braking strides downhill: shorter, quicker steps protect your knees.
Taking on 'just one' rough or slippery section, or a stile: before full clearance, route around it or turn back.
arm_safety: A fall onto the arm is the main risk, so terrain choice is the safety rule: until full clearance, Levels 1–3 ground only (firm, level and stile-free), no slippery or loose ground, and extra care on kerbs and slopes. Keep your uninjured hand free: those routes are flat, so you don't need a pole. Waist pack only until Light use / rehab started. Injured arm relaxed across your stomach (or in its sling if you still wear one). Stop and head home if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you feel dizzy or unusually exhausted. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: Before full clearance: Levels 1–3 walks on free weekends. Phases 4–5: your back-to-back day, building from about 45 min to 3 h on mixed terrain, mostly Zone 1–2

name: Single-arm chest press machine (good arm)
why: Keeps your uninjured arm and chest strong while the other side heals and starts your upper-body muscle gain early. In small trials after wrist and forearm fractures, training the uninjured side helped the injured side keep more strength (the 'cross-education' effect).
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has said you can train your uninjured arm.
Choose a machine with independent arms if possible. Set the seat with your uninjured hand so the handle is at mid-chest height.
Set the weight pin with your uninjured hand and start light.
Sit back with your shoulder blades against the pad, feet flat. Injured arm resting in your lap or across your stomach.
cues: Shoulder blade back and down before you press
Press smoothly and stop just short of locking the elbow
Lower for 2–3 s until you feel a chest stretch
Breathe out as you press
Keep your chest square; don't twist towards the working side
mistakes: Twisting your torso to push: lighter weight, back flat against the pad.
Shoulder shrugging up: set the shoulder blade down and back before each rep.
Injured hand gripping the seat or the other handle: rest it in your lap and keep it open.
arm_safety: Sit down and stand up using your legs; adjust the seat and pin with your uninjured hand (ask staff if a lever is stiff). If the two handles are linked, the unused one may move, so keep your injured arm well clear of it. Injured hand stays open and relaxed in your lap (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one); if you notice it clenching or bracing, reduce the weight. Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Anything your physio prescribes or restricts takes priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm seated cable row (good arm)
equipment: cable machine or seated row station
why: Builds your upper back, the posture muscles that carry a rucksack well, while the one-sided pull trains your core to resist twisting. It also adds to the cross-education effect for the healing arm.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Clip a single D-handle to the low cable (or seated row station) with your uninjured hand and set a light weight.
Sit on the seat or a bench with your feet braced on the footplate or floor, knees soft.
Lean forward to take the handle with your uninjured hand, then sit up tall. Injured arm resting on your thigh or across your stomach.
cues: Sit tall, chest up; no rocking
Pull your elbow back past your ribs, leading with the shoulder blade
Squeeze 1 s, then let the arm reach forward slowly
Shoulders stay square; resist the twist
Breathe out as you pull
mistakes: Leaning back and rocking to move the weight: lighter load, still trunk.
Twisting towards the working side: keep your chest facing forward.
Shrugging: keep the shoulder down, away from your ear.
arm_safety: Seated with your feet braced, so your balance is secure. To finish, let the handle travel forward under control until the stack rests, then let go; never let it snap back. Sit and stand using your legs only. Injured hand open and relaxed on your thigh, well away from the cable (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm lat pulldown (good arm)
equipment: lat pulldown machine or high cable
why: Your lats are among the biggest upper-body muscles, so they matter for the +5 kg goal and for future pull-ups, carries and scrambling. Training one side now keeps the pattern and strength alive until both arms can pull.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Swap the bar for a single D-handle (uninjured hand, or ask staff) and set a light weight.
Set the thigh pad with your uninjured hand so it sits snugly on your thighs.
Stand, take the handle with your uninjured hand, then sit down under the pad, letting the arm stretch overhead. Injured arm resting on your thigh.
cues: Start each rep by drawing the shoulder blade down
Drive the elbow down towards your back pocket
Handle finishes by your shoulder or upper chest
Return slowly over 2–3 s until the arm is long
Stay upright; breathe out as you pull
mistakes: Leaning far back or bending sideways: lighter weight, ribs down.
Pulling with the hand and biceps only: think 'elbow down', not 'hand down'.
Letting the handle snap up: control the return every rep.
arm_safety: Use a weight light enough that sitting down and standing up with the handle is fully controlled. To finish, stand up slowly so the handle rises until the stack rests, then let go. If the handle is out of reach when seated, use a high cable and a bench instead, or ask staff to pass it to you. Injured arm resting on your thigh, hand relaxed and well clear of the pad and cable (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated dumbbell curl (good arm)
why: Builds the elbow flexors and forearm of your uninjured arm, which are part of carrying and farmer strength, and supports the cross-education effect for the healing arm. Sitting with back support keeps you stable and honest.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Set an adjustable bench upright (75–90°) near the dumbbell rack.
Take a light dumbbell from the rack with your uninjured hand, holding it close to your body, and sit down.
Back against the pad, feet flat; injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Elbow stays by your side
Curl up, turning the palm to face you
Squeeze 1 s at the top
Lower over 3 s to a straight arm
Breathe out as you curl
mistakes: Swinging your body: sit back against the pad and lighten the weight.
Elbow drifting forward: keep it pinned by your side.
Half reps: lower all the way down.
arm_safety: Pick up and return the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only, from a rack at hip height where possible rather than the floor. Never pass the dumbbell across your body or near your injured arm. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Single-arm triceps pushdown (good arm)
why: Your triceps make up much of your upper-arm size and will power every press, push-up and pole plant later. This keeps your uninjured arm strong and adds to the cross-education effect.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Pulley at the top; clip on a single D-handle with your uninjured hand and set a light weight.
Stand close to the machine in a short split stance, or sit on a bench under the pulley if you feel at all unsteady.
Elbow tucked by your side; injured arm across your stomach.
cues: Upper arm stays still, pinned to your side
Push down until the elbow is straight and squeeze 1 s
Let the forearm come back up to about 90°, slowly
Stand tall; don't lean over the handle
Breathe out as you push
mistakes: Elbow flaring or drifting forward: lighter weight, elbow glued to your side.
Using your bodyweight to push down: stand tall and let the triceps do it.
Letting the handle fly up: control the return.
arm_safety: A short split stance close to the stack is stable; sit on a bench if you feel at all unsteady. To finish, let the handle rise slowly until the stack rests before letting go. Injured arm across your stomach, hand relaxed and away from the cable (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated single-arm dumbbell shoulder press (good arm)
why: Strong, healthy shoulders matter for swinging a pack onto your back, reaching overhead and, later, carrying. Pressing one side while seated also trains your trunk to stay upright against an uneven load.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Set the bench upright (80–90°). Take a light dumbbell from the rack with your uninjured hand and sit down with it resting on your thigh.
Lift it to shoulder height with your uninjured arm; a small knee lift can help.
Back against the pad, feet wide and flat; injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Ribs down, back against the pad
Press up and slightly in until the arm is straight overhead
Lower over 2–3 s to just above shoulder height
Don't lean away from the dumbbell
Breathe out as you press
mistakes: Arching your lower back: ribs down, lighter weight.
Bending sideways away from the working arm: stay stacked and use less load.
Elbow flared straight out to the side: keep it slightly in front of your body.
arm_safety: Pick up and put down the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only: at the end, lower it to your shoulder, then your thigh, then return it to the rack or lower it to the floor on your uninjured side. If a rep fails, lower it out to your uninjured side, never towards your injured arm. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one). Moderate effort (RIR 2–3) and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Seated wrist curl (good arm)
why: Forearm strength underpins farmer strength, because every carry starts with the grip. Training your uninjured forearm builds that base now, and in a small trial after wrist fractures, training the uninjured wrist was linked with stronger wrist muscles on the injured side once the cast came off.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Sit on a bench and rest your uninjured forearm on your thigh (or along the bench), palm up, wrist just past the knee.
Hold a light dumbbell. Injured arm resting on its own thigh.
Optional: add palm-down (reverse) wrist curls for the extensors.
cues: Forearm stays still on your thigh
Let the wrist bend back slowly; the fingers can uncurl slightly
Curl the wrist up as high as you can and squeeze 1 s
Slow and controlled: 2 s up, 2 s down
mistakes: Lifting the forearm off your thigh: keep it pinned and use a lighter weight.
Bouncing: slow reps through the full range.
Going too heavy: pick a weight you can move smoothly for 12–20 reps.
arm_safety: Seated and stable. Pick up and put down the dumbbell with your uninjured hand only. Injured arm resting on its own thigh, hand open and relaxed (or in its sling if you still wear one); don't let it copy the movement unless your physio has prescribed that. Moderate effort and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.

name: Grip squeeze (good hand)
equipment: hand gripper (about £5–10) or a tightly rolled towel
or a dumbbell for timed holds
why: Grip is the limiting factor in farmer-style carries. Squeezing work builds crushing grip in your uninjured hand now, and in a trial after wrist fractures, training the uninjured hand was linked with better grip strength in the injured hand at 12 weeks.
setup: Only once your clinic or physio has cleared you to train your uninjured arm.
Sit on a bench with your uninjured forearm resting on your thigh.
Hold a gripper, stress ball or tightly rolled towel in your uninjured hand. In the gym, a timed hold of a dumbbell hanging at your side while seated works too.
Injured arm resting on its own thigh.
cues: Squeeze hard for 3–5 s, then relax fully
Wrist straight, thumb wrapped round
Breathe out as you squeeze; no breath-holding
For holds: shoulder down, sit tall, hold for time
mistakes: Holding your breath while squeezing: breathe out slowly through each squeeze.
Bending the wrist: keep it straight and strong.
Partial squeezes: close the hand fully (or as far as the gripper allows) and hold.
arm_safety: Seated and stable. Keep your injured hand open and relaxed on its thigh (or the arm in its sling if you still wear one); you may notice it wants to squeeze too, so let it rest. If your physio has prescribed hand exercises for your injured side, do those separately, as prescribed. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom.
dose: 3 × 8–12 hard 3-s squeezes, RIR 2–3

name: Suitcase carry (good hand)
equipment: dumbbell (or kettlebell if your gym has them)
why: A one-sided carry makes your core keep you upright and walking straight, and it builds grip. It isn't in your plan: training carries wait for grip clearance, and with your uninjured hand holding the weight nothing is free to break a stumble. After grip clearance, do it only if your physio suggests a one-handed carry with your uninjured hand while your injured hand builds up.
setup: Only after grip clearance (training carries wait for it), and only if your physio suggests carrying with your uninjured hand alone.
Choose a clear, flat 15–20 m lane with nothing to trip over.
Take the dumbbell from a rack at hip height with your uninjured hand (or pick it up from the floor with a flat back, bending your knees).
Stand tall; injured arm resting across your stomach.
cues: Stand tall; don't lean towards or away from the weight
Shoulders level; pull the carrying shoulder down and back
Brace lightly and keep breathing
Normal, steady steps; eyes ahead
Squeeze the handle hard
mistakes: Leaning away from the weight to balance it: lighter dumbbell, stand tall.
Shrugging the carrying shoulder: pull it down towards your back pocket.
Rushing: walk at a normal pace, because speed hides poor posture.
arm_safety: Normally your uninjured hand is your fall protection, and here it's holding the weight, so if you stumble, drop the dumbbell to the side straight away and keep your injured arm tucked in. Flat, clear, dry floor only; turn slowly at the end of each length. Put the dumbbell down by squatting with a flat back. Once your injured hand reaches the 70% rung (measured by your physio or with their OK), the both-sides suitcase carry replaces this one. Moderate load and no breath-holding. Physio instructions take priority. Stop if your injured arm aches, throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, you notice any red-flag symptom, or you feel unsteady. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: 3–4 × 20–30 m; start light (around 8–12 kg) and add 2 kg when you can walk tall with no lean

name: Finger tendon glides (injured hand)
equipment: table or pillow to support the forearm
why: Typical purpose: keeps the finger tendons sliding freely through the wrist and forearm and helps with finger stiffness, which is the starting point for getting your grip, and so your farmer strength, back. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table with your forearm supported, elbow bent, wrist relaxed and roughly straight.

Move slowly through five positions: straight hand; hook fist (bend the middle and end finger joints, knuckles straight); full fist; tabletop (bend at the knuckles only, fingers straight); straight fist (bend the knuckles and middle joints, fingertips straight, touching the base of your palm).
Return to the straight hand between positions if your physio prefers.
cues: Slow and gentle; hold each position 3–5 s
Move only as far as is comfortable
Keep the wrist relaxed and still
Breathe normally
mistakes: Forcing the fist with the other hand: active movement only, unless your physio has shown you otherwise.
Rushing through the positions: each one moves the tendons differently, so take your time.
Pushing into sharp pain: back off to a comfortable range.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Sit with the forearm fully supported. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 5–10 slow rounds, several times a day.

name: Wrist bend up and down (active range of motion)
why: Typical purpose: restores the up-and-down bend of the wrist (flexion and extension), which you'll need for everything from getting up off the floor to carrying and using walking poles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table and rest your forearm on a folded towel, hand over the edge, palm down.
Let your fingers relax, or make a loose fist if your physio prefers.
cues: Slowly lift the back of your hand up as far as is comfortable
Then slowly lower it down as far as is comfortable
Forearm stays flat on the towel
Smooth movement with a brief pause at each end
Repeat palm up only if your physio prescribes it
mistakes: Lifting the forearm to cheat the range: keep it pinned to the towel.
Forcing the end of the range with the other hand: only if your physio has taught you assisted stretches.
Fast, jerky reps: slow and smooth.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported throughout. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps, 3–4 times a day.

name: Forearm rotation (palm up, palm down)
equipment: table or thigh to support the forearm
why: Typical purpose: restores turning the palm up (supination) and down (pronation). This movement depends on both forearm bones, so it's a common focus of rehab after forearm fractures, and you need it for door handles, keys, mugs and walking poles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your elbow bent to 90° and tucked into your side; a rolled towel between elbow and ribs helps.
Forearm supported on a table or your thigh, thumb pointing up.
cues: Slowly turn your palm up to face the ceiling
Then slowly turn it down to face the floor
Elbow stays tucked in; don't let the shoulder do the work
Pause briefly at each end of the comfortable range
mistakes: Elbow drifting away from your body: keep the towel squeezed against your side.
Rotating from the shoulder to fake the range: keep the upper arm still.
Pushing into sharp pain: stay in the comfortable range.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported and the movement slow. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps each way, 3–4 times a day.

name: Wrist side to side (radial and ulnar deviation)
muscles: wrist flexors and extensors (thumb side and little-finger side)
why: Typical purpose: restores the side-to-side movement of the wrist, which you use when pouring, hammering, gripping a walking pole and carrying a bag by its handle. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit with your forearm resting on a table, palm down and hand flat (or thumb up with the hand over the edge, if that's what your physio shows you).
Keep the forearm still.
cues: Slide your hand towards the thumb side, then towards the little-finger side
Keep the movement at the wrist, not the elbow
Slow and smooth, with a brief pause at each end
Only as far as is comfortable
mistakes: Moving the forearm instead of the wrist: anchor the forearm on the table.
Bending the wrist up or down at the same time: keep the hand flat on the table.
Rushing: slow reps.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Keep the forearm supported. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps each way, 3–4 times a day.

name: Elbow bend and straighten (active range of motion)
why: Typical purpose: keeps or restores full elbow bending and straightening, which can stiffen after a forearm fracture and a period of protecting the arm. A straight elbow matters for carrying, and a full bend for eating and washing. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit or stand tall with your upper arm by your side, or supported on a table if your physio prefers.
Start with the palm facing up; your physio may also ask for palm-down or thumb-up versions.
cues: Slowly bend the elbow, bringing your hand towards your shoulder
Then slowly straighten it as far as is comfortable
Shoulder relaxed and still
Pause briefly at each end
mistakes: Swinging the arm: slow, controlled movement.
Shrugging the shoulder: keep it down and relaxed.
Forcing the last few degrees: stay gentle; consistency beats force.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Move slowly and don't swing the arm. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 10 slow reps, 3–4 times a day.

name: Therapy putty grip work
equipment: therapy putty (grade chosen by your physio)
why: Typical purpose: an early step in rebuilding grip strength, with resistance that can be fine-tuned. Grip is the base of your farmer-strength goal, so this is where that journey restarts for your injured hand. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table with your forearm supported.
Use the putty grade your physio gives you, usually the softest to begin with.
Common drills: full-hand squeeze; pinching between the thumb and each fingertip; spreading the fingers against a putty ring.
cues: Squeeze slowly and steadily, then relax fully
Re-form the putty into a ball between sets
Wrist straight and relaxed
Quality over quantity
mistakes: Using putty that's too firm: start soft and progress only when your physio says so.
Squeezing hard and fast to exhaustion: slow, controlled squeezes.
Wrist bending as you squeeze: keep it in line with your forearm.
arm_safety: Do this only if your physio or clinic has prescribed it, and only the way they showed you. Never move up a putty grade on your own. Your physio will tell you how much discomfort is acceptable. Stop and contact your physio or fracture clinic (or NHS 111 out of hours) if pain is sharp or keeps increasing, the hand or forearm swells more, goes numb, tingly, pale, blue or cold, the wound or scar looks red, hot or weeps, or you feel feverish or unwell.
dose: Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders. Typical starting point: 2–3 sets of 10 squeezes, once or twice a day.

name: Towel wringing
equipment: small hand towel (dry unless your physio says otherwise)
why: Typical purpose: combines grip with forearm rotation in both directions, a practical step towards wringing cloths, opening jars and handling ropes and handles. Only as prescribed by your physio; doses here are placeholders.
setup: Use only the version your physio has shown you.
Sit at a table and roll a small towel into a tube.
Hold it with both hands in front of you, elbows bent and close to your sides.
cues: Twist gently in one direction, as if wringing water out
Then twist the other way

name: Light ruck (walking with a light rucksack)
equipment: rucksack with hip belt and sternum strap
light load (water bottles, a bag of rice, or a small plate wrapped in a towel)
why: Long-distance hiking means carrying a pack for hours. Starting very light lets your feet, legs, back and shoulders adapt gradually, so that proper hiking loads feel normal later.
setup: Only once your clinic has cleared you for light use of your injured arm.
Start with 2–4 kg, and keep it light (no more than about 10% of your bodyweight) until full clearance.
Pack the weight high and close to your back, and pad any hard objects.
Fit: hip belt on top of your hip bones carrying most of the load, shoulder straps snug, sternum strap clipped.
Route: incline treadmill or good, even paths, with the same terrain rules as your hikes.
cues: Tall posture with a very slight lean from the ankles
Short, steady steps, especially downhill
Your hips carry the load, not your shoulders
Stay in Zone 2: you can talk but would rather not
Add about 1 kg every 2–3 weeks, only if the walk and the next morning felt fine
mistakes: Adding weight and distance in the same week: change one thing at a time.
Loose hip belt, so the load hangs off your shoulders: tighten it on your hip bones.
Hunching forward: lighten the pack and stand tall.
arm_safety: Putting it on, seated: sit on a bench with the pack beside you, slide your uninjured arm through its strap and lift the pack onto your back with that arm, then ease your injured arm into the other strap without gripping or pushing; fasten the hip belt and sternum strap with your uninjured hand, then stand. Taking it off: sit down, unclip with your uninjured hand, slide the strap off your injured side first, then lower the pack with your uninjured arm. Never swing it on or off. Check that no strap rubs or presses on a scar or the fracture site. A pack makes a stumble harder to recover from, so the terrain rules are strict: even surfaces, no ice, mud or loose ground, and extra care on descents. Stop if arm pain rises, it throbs, swells, tingles or goes numb, or you notice any red-flag symptom. Any fall onto the arm: stop and get it checked.
dose: Your Saturday long walk: 80 min in Zone 2 with 2–4 kg to start, adding about 1 kg every 2–3 weeks if the walk and next morning feel fine; keep it to about 10% of your body weight (8 kg for the 80 kg example profile) until full clearance
